# U5-C01 - Lord Kelvin and Joseph Black

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Explain what a thermometer measures; distinguish sensible and latent heating; connect Black’s measurements to calorimetry and Kelvin’s temperature ideas to gas ratios and engine limits.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## Two questions that temperature alone cannot answer
Put a small cup and a large bucket of water in the same room overnight. They can reach the same temperature, but warming the bucket by another degree requires more energy. Now place melting ice and liquid water together. Energy can enter while their temperature remains nearly constant. These familiar situations expose a basic difficulty: a thermometer reading does not tell us the total energy transferred or stored. Joseph Black’s work helped clarify this distinction long before the modern first law had taken shape.

There is a different difficulty with temperature scales. A reading of 20 °C is not twice the thermodynamic temperature of 10 °C. Celsius assigns its zero by convention; it does not begin at the lower limit of ordinary thermodynamic temperature. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, helped develop an absolute scale linked to general thermal principles rather than to one particular thermometer substance. Black and Kelvin therefore addressed related but different measurement problems.

## Black: observations before a complete energy theory
Joseph Black lived from 1728 to 1799 and taught chemistry at Glasgow and Edinburgh. During his Glasgow work he developed ideas about latent heat and specific heat, describing his investigations publicly in 1762. His lectures were influential, but their collected publication in 1803 was posthumous. The publication date should not be mistaken for the date of the discoveries. [H01]

Black’s surviving lectures discuss the slow melting of ice and the different thermal effects of different substances. They also discuss earlier experiments by other investigators. This matters historically: scientific progress included interpreting existing observations, not only inventing new equipment. Black argued that equal thermometer readings could not be treated as equal quantities of heat. His language sometimes treated heat as a material substance. We retain the experimental distinctions while translating their explanation into modern energy language. [H02]

## Why melting ice can absorb energy without warming
Imagine supplying a steady, measured amount of energy to pure ice already at its melting point, at approximately atmospheric pressure. As long as ice and water coexist under these conditions, the mixture remains close to 0 °C. The added energy changes the phase rather than producing the usual temperature rise. The molecular arrangement changes; energy is associated with the changed interactions and structure. It is not correct to say that the heater has stopped transferring energy because the thermometer has stopped rising.

The modern relationship Q=mL describes this idealized phase change. Q is transferred energy in joules, m is mass in kilograms, and L is specific latent heat in joules per kilogram. For melting, Q is positive into the material. For freezing the same mass under comparable conditions, energy leaves. The word latent means that the transfer is not revealed by a temperature rise during the phase change; it does not mean energy has vanished or become impossible to measure.

Once all the ice has melted, continued input can warm the liquid. For a modest temperature interval with no phase change, Q=mcΔT is a useful model. Here c is specific heat capacity in J/(kg·K). Different substances generally have different c values. A sample’s heat capacity C=mc is in J/K and also depends on its mass. A conductivity value, in W/(m·K), answers a different question about the rate of heat flow through a material. Black’s legacy connects especially to capacity and phase energy, not to identifying the fastest conductor.

## Calorimetry: infer a transfer from an energy balance
Calorimetry means measuring energy transfer through controlled thermal changes. In an insulated mixing experiment, the warmer object loses energy while the cooler object and container gain it. Temperatures, masses and suitable heat-capacity data let us balance those transfers. If the container absorbs appreciable energy, ignoring it introduces an error. If equal masses of the same liquid are mixed with negligible losses and constant c, their final temperature lies halfway between the starting temperatures. With unequal masses or different materials, a simple average is generally wrong.

This reasoning does not require calling the material a container of stored heat. In modern terminology, heat names a transfer caused by a temperature difference; internal energy is a state property. Black’s historical vocabulary is evidence about his period, not permission to abandon the precise definitions from Unit 1. A scientifically strong historical explanation can admire a measurement while correcting the old model used to interpret it.

## Kelvin: an absolute scale and the laws of thermodynamics
William Thomson lived from 1824 to 1907 and became a professor at Glasgow. His 1848 paper proposed an absolute thermometric scale. The first proposal was not identical to the modern linear Kelvin scale; his temperature ideas developed further as energy-based thermodynamics matured. He also worked on the limits of converting heat into work and collaborated with Joule on gas investigations. These are documented connections, rather than a claim that the two developed every law together. [H03]

The modern conversion is T=t+273.15, where T is in kelvins and t is in degrees Celsius. A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C, but the zeros differ. Use K without a degree symbol. A temperature difference can therefore be expressed with either degree size, whereas an absolute-temperature ratio in the ideal-gas law or Carnot bound must use Kelvin values.

Absolute zero is 0 K, corresponding to −273.15 °C. It represents the lower limit approached by ordinary positive-temperature equilibrium systems. Do not picture it as the disappearance of all energy, all particles or every kind of motion. Modern quantum physics allows ground-state energy and quantum motion; temperature alone also does not specify all stored energy. The detailed third-law treatment belongs to the State/National Unit 6. This chapter supplies the historical context without assessing that advanced law.

## Compare contributions by the question answered
Black helps us ask, “How much energy is required for this material change?” Kelvin helps us ask, “How should thermodynamic temperature be measured consistently?” A phase-change calculation may use Black-associated concepts without any Kelvin ratio. An engine-limit calculation needs absolute temperatures even if no material melts. Neither scientist’s contribution makes the other unnecessary.

Today thermodynamic temperature is tied to a fixed value of the Boltzmann constant in the SI. That is a modern refinement of measurement, not something Kelvin wrote in 1848. [H04] Engineers using cryogenic sensors, scientists measuring gas behavior, and students comparing reservoirs all benefit from an absolute scale. Cooling packs and thermal storage materials instead make especially visible the distinction between energy transfer and temperature change.

## Visual model
![Two panels connect a melting plateau to energy input and compare Celsius with Kelvin. Plateau data are illustrative; both scale columns refer to the same physical temperatures.](figures/U5-C01.svg)

Two panels connect a melting plateau to energy input and compare Celsius with Kelvin. Plateau data are illustrative; both scale columns refer to the same physical temperatures.

## Important terminology
Thermodynamic temperature: absolute temperature, K. Specific heat capacity c: energy per mass per temperature change, J/(kg·K). Heat capacity C: sample coefficient, J/K. Specific latent heat L: energy per mass for a specified phase change, J/kg. Calorimetry: measurement through thermal energy accounting.

## Worked example: A scale suitable for ratios

**Given:** A sample is at 26.85 °C.

**Find:** Its absolute temperature.

**Formula:** T=t+273.15.

**Substitution:** T=26.85+273.15 K.

**Calculation:** 26.85+273.15=300.00.

**Final answer:** T=300.00 K.

**Physical interpretation:** The offset changes the zero, not the size of one temperature step.

## Worked example: Equal temperature rise, different material

**Given:** Two 0.20 kg samples warm by 5.0 K; c_A=4200 and c_B=900 J/(kg·K). No phase change or loss.

**Find:** Energy needed by each.

**Formula:** Q=mcΔT.

**Substitution:** Q_A=0.20×4200×5.0; Q_B=0.20×900×5.0.

**Calculation:** Q_A=4200; Q_B=900.

**Final answer:** A needs 4200 J; B needs 900 J.

**Physical interpretation:** Equal mass and temperature rise do not imply equal energy transfer. This is the distinction associated with specific heat.

## Worked example: Energy on the melting plateau

**Given:** 0.050 kg ice melts at 0 °C; L=334000 J/kg; ignore losses.

**Find:** Energy absorbed.

**Formula:** Q=mL.

**Substitution:** Q=0.050×334000 J.

**Calculation:** Q=16700.

**Final answer:** Q=16700 J, or 16.7 kJ.

**Physical interpretation:** A zero temperature rise does not imply zero heat transfer during melting.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
Black did not invent the Kelvin scale. Kelvin did not discover latent heat. Equal temperature is not equal internal energy. The 1803 lecture publication is not Black working after his death. The modern SI definition and quantum account of absolute zero must not be projected backward into the 1848 paper.

## Application and safe investigation
Use a teacher-prepared ice-water data table or observe a small open cup with a room-temperature thermometer under adult supervision. Do not reproduce historical mercury experiments. Record phase and temperature together: a single temperature trace cannot establish whether the mixture is still melting. Compare equal masses using supplied c values rather than assuming heating-rate differences measure conductivity alone.

## Chapter summary
Black separated temperature from the amount of thermal transfer, making phase changes and material-specific heating clearer. Kelvin helped develop an absolute temperature framework connected to general thermodynamics. Modern equations express these contributions with later refinements, consistent units and explicit assumptions.

## Chapter review
1. Why can melting ice absorb energy with little temperature change?
2. Why is 20 °C not twice 10 °C on an absolute scale?
3. How can a historical observation remain valuable after its explanation changes?

## Practice
[WS29](../worksheets/WS29.md) includes eight questions from recognition to evidence-based reasoning.

## Mastery checklist
- [ ] I can distinguish Black’s and Kelvin’s contributions.
- [ ] I can choose Q=mL or Q=mcΔT and state the conditions.
- [ ] I can separate a historical date from a later publication or refinement.

## Historical evidence
H01: Edinburgh history of Black; H02: Black’s lectures, published 1803; H03: MacTutor biography of Thomson; H04: BIPM Kelvin definition.

Full bibliographic details, links and attribution limits: [Unit 5 source guide](../references/U5-sources.md).

chapters.content_markdown:
# U5-C02 - James Prescott Joule and Sadi Carnot

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Interpret work-to-warming experiments; use the first law consistently; explain reversible engine limits; distinguish Carnot’s original caloric framework from modern energy accounting.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## Two engine questions with different answers
Suppose a workshop uses a heat engine to lift a load. How many joules enter, leave and become work? That is an energy-accounting question. Could an improved engine convert every incoming joule into work during a complete cycle? That is a performance-limit question. Joule’s work strongly supported the quantitative relationship between mechanical work and thermal effects. Carnot’s analysis identified a general structure for ideal engine performance. The modern first and second laws combine these ideas without making them identical.

## Joule: careful measurements of very small warming
James Prescott Joule lived from 1818 to 1889 and worked in the Manchester area. In the 1840s he investigated ways that mechanical and electrical processes produced thermal changes. A famous arrangement used falling weights to turn paddles in water. The water’s temperature rose slightly. Repetition, careful thermometry and attention to other energy destinations were essential because the rise was small. The Science and Industry Museum describes this experimental program; its collection also contains a later paddlewheel, dated approximately 1860. A museum object’s date is not automatically the date of the first discovery. [H05]

Follow the energy rather than just the thermometer. Raised weights have gravitational potential energy. As they descend, that energy can be transferred through the apparatus as mechanical work. The paddles stir the water. Viscous effects convert organized motion into microscopic energy, and the water warms. If the water is the chosen system, the paddle interaction is work entering it. It is not heat entering merely because the result is a higher temperature. Heat may subsequently leave through the container to the room.

Joule’s repeated measurements helped establish a consistent mechanical equivalent for a specified thermal change. The result challenged the idea that heat was simply an indestructible fluid that could only be moved around. Energy conservation emerged through the work of multiple investigators; Joule was a major experimental contributor, not the sole person responsible for every statement of the first law. In modern SI, the same energy unit measures work, heat transfer and internal-energy change. One joule is one newton-meter of work when force and displacement are aligned.

## Reconstruct the reasoning, not the historical apparatus
For a teaching model, suppose a known amount of paddle work enters a thermally insulated vessel. If no energy leaves and bulk motion has settled, the water-plus-vessel internal energy rises by that input. Our convention remains ΔU=Q−W, with W positive by the system. Work done on the system is negative W. If Q=0 and W=−600 J, then ΔU=+600 J.

The sample may then obey ΔU=CΔT with a supplied heat capacity C in J/K. A complete experiment needs the vessel and paddle heat capacities, transfer losses, and measurement uncertainty. Measuring the water alone can undercount energy if the container also warms. A small discrepancy is a reason to improve the accounting, not instant evidence that energy conservation failed. These controls connect historical experimentation to the practical data work in Units 3 and 7.

## Carnot: the problem of the best possible engine
Sadi Carnot lived from 1796 to 1832 and trained as a French military engineer. In 1824 he published his study of the motive power of heat. It was motivated by engines and their performance, but its importance was broader than improving a single machine. He considered idealized reversible operation and the temperatures between which an engine works. Clapeyron’s 1834 reformulation helped communicate the work; Clausius and Thomson later incorporated its insights into energy-based thermodynamics. [H06]

Carnot’s published analysis used the caloric framework, which treated heat as a conserved substance passing from a warmer body to a cooler one. Modern thermodynamics instead allows some absorbed energy to leave as work, so the heat rejected by a cyclic engine is less than the heat absorbed by the net work output. We should not pretend that Carnot’s 1824 book already used today’s complete energy ledger. His valuable ideas about reversible limits survived the replacement of that framework.

## The modern Carnot engine as an ideal comparison
A reservoir is idealized as large enough to exchange heat without appreciably changing temperature. A modern Carnot cycle contains two reversible isothermal stages and two reversible adiabatic stages. During hot isothermal expansion, a suitable working gas absorbs heat and does work while maintaining temperature. Adiabatic expansion lowers its temperature without heat transfer. Cold isothermal compression rejects heat. Adiabatic compression returns the gas to the starting temperature and state. This is a conceptual sequence; no curved-path work integral is required.

Reversible means that the process could be undone without a net change to both system and surroundings. Merely moving slowly is insufficient if friction or finite temperature differences still produce irreversibility. A truly reversible cycle is an ideal limiting model. It is useful because it tells us a ceiling that improved materials alone cannot exceed between the same reservoirs.

With Q_H and Q_C positive magnitudes, a cyclic engine satisfies W_net=Q_H−Q_C. Its actual thermal efficiency is η=W_net/Q_H. The modern reversible upper bound is η_max=1−T_C/T_H, with reservoir temperatures in Kelvin. An actual engine usually performs below this bound. The equation belongs to the later mature thermodynamic interpretation of Carnot’s insight, not a claim that his original notation and physical assumptions matched ours.

## Why conservation does not promise complete conversion
An engine taking 1000 J from a hot reservoir and rejecting 700 J can provide 300 J of net work. The rejected energy has not been destroyed. It enters the colder surroundings. A claim of 1000 J work and no rejected heat could balance a first-law ledger, but for a cyclic engine operating with ordinary finite positive-temperature reservoirs it fails the second-law limit. Returning the working substance to its starting state is essential; one expansion stroke is not a whole engine cycle.

The first law asks how much energy is transferred. The second law restricts its possible redistribution and usefulness. This is why Joule and Carnot belong together in a conceptual history but must not be merged into a single discovery. One gives a quantitative bridge between transfer modes; the other supplies the roots of a limit on useful conversion.

## Visual model
![Left: work from descending weights enters a stirred sample. Right: a modern cyclic engine divides heat input into net work and rejected heat. Arrows are conceptual, not proportional.](figures/U5-C02.svg)

Left: work from descending weights enters a stirred sample. Right: a modern cyclic engine divides heat input into net work and rejected heat. Arrows are conceptual, not proportional.

## Important terminology
Mechanical equivalent of heat: quantitative equivalence between mechanical input and a specified thermal effect. Caloric theory: historical conserved-heat-substance model. Reservoir: nearly fixed-temperature thermal source or sink. Reversible cycle: ideal cycle with no net irreversible effects. Efficiency η: useful net work divided by absorbed heat, dimensionless.

## Worked example: Paddles warm an insulated sample

**Given:** Work input=840 J; Q=0; total C=420 J/K; no bulk energy change.

**Find:** ΔU and ΔT.

**Formula:** ΔU=Q−W; ΔT=ΔU/C.

**Substitution:** ΔU=0−(−840); ΔT=840/420.

**Calculation:** ΔU=840; ΔT=2.0.

**Final answer:** ΔU=+840 J; ΔT=+2.0 K.

**Physical interpretation:** Mechanical work can warm a sample without incoming heat.

## Worked example: An engine ledger

**Given:** Q_H=1200 J; Q_C=840 J per cycle.

**Find:** Net work and efficiency.

**Formula:** W_net=Q_H−Q_C; η=W_net/Q_H.

**Substitution:** W_net=1200−840; η=360/1200.

**Calculation:** W_net=360; η=0.30.

**Final answer:** W_net=360 J; η=30%.

**Physical interpretation:** The other 70% is rejected energy, not missing energy.

## Worked example: A modern ideal ceiling

**Given:** T_H=500 K; T_C=300 K; actual η=30%.

**Find:** Maximum efficiency and comparison.

**Formula:** η_max=1−T_C/T_H.

**Substitution:** η_max=1−300/500.

**Calculation:** 1−0.60=0.40.

**Final answer:** Maximum=40%; 30% is below the bound.

**Physical interpretation:** Passing this necessary limit does not prove every feature of a proposed design feasible.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
Joule’s paddle work is not incoming heat merely because water warms. Carnot did not build a practical frictionless engine. The modern Carnot equation is not a complete description of the 1824 framework. Engine efficiency is not output power, and rejected energy is not destroyed energy.

## Application and safe investigation
Use supplied data for paddle-work experiments; falling masses, shafts and improvised steam engines are unnecessary. A safe paper activity assigns energy cards to water, vessel and surroundings. Students find which omitted destination explains a mismatch. For engine examples, compare actual η and the Kelvin-based bound before discussing a possible improvement.

## Chapter summary
Joule connected mechanical input to measurable thermal change. Carnot analyzed ideal engine performance in a framework later corrected by energy conservation. Modern thermodynamics preserves the useful reversible insight while accounting for heat input, heat rejection and work in common energy units.

## Chapter review
1. Why is paddling water work rather than heat transfer into it?
2. Which part of Carnot’s historical framework had to change?
3. How can an engine conserve energy and still be impossible?

## Practice
[WS30](../worksheets/WS30.md) includes eight questions from recognition to evidence-based reasoning.

## Mastery checklist
- [ ] I can account for work-on signs.
- [ ] I can distinguish actual efficiency from its ideal upper bound.
- [ ] I can explain a surviving insight without retaining an obsolete model.

## Historical evidence
H05: Science and Industry Museum experimental history and collection record; H06: MacTutor history of Carnot; H03 and H07 support the later Thomson/Clausius development.

Full bibliographic details, links and attribution limits: [Unit 5 source guide](../references/U5-sources.md).

chapters.title: Max Planck and Rudolf Clausius
chapters.objectives: Explain why a radiation spectrum challenged classical models; describe energy quantization at an introductory level; connect Clausius’s entropy to irreversible processes and distinguish it from energy.
chapters.content_markdown:
# U5-C03 - Max Planck and Rudolf Clausius

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Explain why a radiation spectrum challenged classical models; describe energy quantization at an introductory level; connect Clausius’s entropy to irreversible processes and distinguish it from energy.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## From visible effects to limits on a theory
Heat can move through empty space, as Unit 3 explained. A hot object emits electromagnetic radiation across a range of wavelengths. But recognizing radiation as a transfer mechanism does not yet tell us how much is emitted at each wavelength. That distribution is a spectrum. Explaining its measured shape became a major theoretical problem. Planck’s work on this problem opened a route toward quantum physics.

Clausius addressed a different gap. Conservation says that energy balances, but it does not explain why a warm mug cools in a cooler room rather than becoming hotter while the room cools. His work on heat, work and cycles helped develop the second law and the state quantity entropy. These two scientists are paired here because each exposed a limit of a simpler description; they did not discover the same quantity.

## Clausius: connect conservation with direction
Rudolf Clausius lived from 1822 to 1888. His important 1850 paper helped reconcile Carnot’s engine reasoning with the conversion of heat and work. In 1865 he named and defined entropy after years of development of the concept. The second law did not suddenly appear in finished form on one day; these dates identify important stages. [H07]

An introductory Clausius-style statement says that heat does not pass from a colder body to a warmer one as the sole result of a process. The phrase “sole result” matters. A refrigerator transfers energy out of a cold interior and into a warmer room, but it also uses work input. Include the power supply and the room and there is no contradiction. Omitting them creates a false puzzle by drawing the system boundary too narrowly.

Entropy S is a state property with units J/K. It is not the same as energy U in joules. For an isolated combination, the total entropy cannot decrease; an ideal reversible process leaves it unchanged, whereas an irreversible process increases it. A subsystem can lose entropy as long as the full accounting is consistent. A cooling cup can lose entropy while the room gains more.

## Irreversibility and a complete cycle
Imagine stirring cream into coffee. Energy still balances, but the original separated arrangement does not spontaneously reappear on a kitchen timescale. Real heat conduction across a temperature difference, friction and mixing provide familiar examples of irreversible change. “Irreversible” does not mean no component can ever be restored. A machine could separate or cool materials again, but the restoration would leave changes elsewhere, such as work consumption and energy release.

A working gas completing a cycle returns to its initial internal energy and entropy. The surroundings need not return to their initial state. Therefore an engine can have ΔS_gas=0 each cycle while the complete system-plus-surroundings entropy increases. This resolves a common confusion: repeating a cycle is not the same as reversing it without consequences. Clausius’s state-property approach helps track what returns and what does not.

## Planck: explaining the whole radiation spectrum
Max Planck lived from 1858 to 1947. In 1900 he developed the radiation law associated with his name and introduced discrete energy elements in the statistical treatment of matter oscillators exchanging energy with radiation. His work was recognized with the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics. That prize date is later than the scientific breakthrough. [H08]

A blackbody is an ideal absorber of incident electromagnetic radiation; in thermal equilibrium its emission spectrum depends on its temperature. The word black does not mean it emits no light. A sufficiently hot blackbody can glow brightly. A small opening into a suitable cavity approximates blackbody behavior because incident light undergoes repeated interactions with the interior. This is historical context under the all-level history syllabus; detailed radiant-exitance, blackbody and Stefan–Boltzmann calculations are reserved for Unit 6.

The classical problem concerned the failure of existing models to describe the measured spectrum across all frequencies. A classical equipartition treatment led to an unphysical unlimited high-frequency contribution. The familiar label “ultraviolet catastrophe” describes this failure, but should not be treated as the exact slogan that motivated every step of Planck’s 1900 work. Measurements and the search for a valid spectrum were central. A model can fit one region yet fail elsewhere; agreement with part of a graph is not enough.

## What an energy quantum means here
In the introductory modern notation ε=hf, one energy element ε has units J, frequency f has units Hz or cycles per second, and Planck’s constant h has units J·s. Frequency is the number of oscillations per second; it is not brightness. In the simplified oscillator account, allowed energy exchanges involve multiples of an element whose size depends on frequency. A staircase is a useful analogy for discrete steps, but its steps are not literal pieces of matter.

We do not need to calculate photon energies or derive a spectrum in this unit. The key relation is conceptual: higher frequency corresponds to a larger energy element. Doubling frequency doubles that element; it does not necessarily double the total power from a lamp, because the number and distribution of emitted quanta also matter. Nor does quantization mean all energies in every physical situation must be identical-sized packets.

Do not attribute the entire later photon picture to Planck alone. Einstein’s 1905 light-quantum proposal extended the development. Nobel’s historical discussion explicitly distinguishes Planck’s discovery of energy quanta from credit for the particle nature of light. [H09] Planck’s 1900 framework was a beginning, not a finished version of modern quantum mechanics.

## What joins these contributions
Clausius gave a macroscopic way to reason about entropy and the direction of processes. Later statistical work linked entropy to microscopic possibilities, and Planck used statistical reasoning in his radiation problem. This is an intellectual connection across developments, not evidence that Clausius and Planck jointly ran a blackbody experiment. We must distinguish a documented influence from a classroom map of related concepts.

Today we use energy balances and entropy limits together when evaluating machines. We also use quantum-based radiation models when interpreting glowing materials and thermal spectra. Neither development invalidates energy conservation. Instead, each adds information that an energy total alone cannot provide: which directions are possible, or how energy is distributed among microscopic modes and radiation frequencies.

## Visual model
![A qualitative spectrum has a finite peak, whereas the illustrated failing classical trend rises at short wavelength. A separate entropy ledger shows a local decrease and larger surroundings increase. No spectral numbers are assessed.](figures/U5-C03.svg)

A qualitative spectrum has a finite peak, whereas the illustrated failing classical trend rises at short wavelength. A separate entropy ledger shows a local decrease and larger surroundings increase. No spectral numbers are assessed.

## Important terminology
Spectrum: distribution of radiation over wavelength or frequency. Blackbody: ideal absorber with a temperature-dependent equilibrium emission spectrum. Quantum: discrete energy element in the specified model. Entropy S: thermodynamic state property, J/K. Irreversibility: production of entropy in complete accounting. Frequency f: cycles per second, Hz.

## Worked example: Energy accounting in a refrigerator

**Given:** Work input=200 J; heat removed from cold interior=500 J per cycle.

**Find:** Heat delivered to room.

**Formula:** Q_room=Q_cold+W_on for the complete cycle.

**Substitution:** Q_room=500+200 J.

**Calculation:** 500+200=700.

**Final answer:** Q_room=700 J.

**Physical interpretation:** Cold-to-hot transfer has an additional effect: work is consumed and ultimately also reaches the room.

## Worked example: Use a supplied entropy ledger

**Given:** Cup ΔS=−2 J/K; room ΔS=+3 J/K; these are all affected parts.

**Find:** Total entropy change and allowed direction.

**Formula:** ΔS_total=ΔS_cup+ΔS_room.

**Substitution:** ΔS_total=−2+3 J/K.

**Calculation:** −2+3=1.

**Final answer:** ΔS_total=+1 J/K.

**Physical interpretation:** A local entropy decrease is compatible with an irreversible total increase; this does not calculate energy loss.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
Entropy is not a quantity of energy that disappears. A refrigerator does not refute the second law. Planck did not introduce the word entropy, and Clausius did not discover quanta. Blackbody does not mean non-emitting. The Nobel award year is not the 1900 discovery year. Historical context is not an invitation to assess State/National radiation equations early.

## Application and safe investigation
Compare supplied spectrum sketches and identify where a model fails; do not heat metal or look into bright lamps. Use a paper refrigerator ledger to show why its room receives both the removed energy and input work. Discuss an ordinary thermal camera as a radiation application while noting that surface properties and calibration affect readings.

## Chapter summary
Clausius extended heat-engine reasoning into the second law and entropy. Planck’s radiation problem required discrete energy elements and opened quantum physics. Both developments show why balancing total energy is essential but insufficient to explain all thermal phenomena.

## Chapter review
1. Why does refrigerator operation require a wider system boundary?
2. What does a radiation spectrum show that a single total-energy value does not?
3. Why should Planck’s contribution be distinguished from later photon theory?

## Practice
[WS31](../worksheets/WS31.md) includes eight questions from recognition to evidence-based reasoning.

## Mastery checklist
- [ ] I can state Clausius’s contribution and the importance of total entropy.
- [ ] I can explain the radiation problem without advanced calculations.
- [ ] I can distinguish discovery, later interpretation and award dates.

## Historical evidence
H07: Clausius chronology; H08: Nobel facts for Planck; H09: Nobel historical discussion of quanta and the later light-quantum interpretation.

Full bibliographic details, links and attribution limits: [Unit 5 source guide](../references/U5-sources.md).

chapters.title: Ludwig Boltzmann and James Clerk Maxwell
chapters.objectives: Connect microscopic motion to macroscopic gas properties; read a speed distribution; use a small counting model to explain multiplicity; distinguish statistical entropy from a vague claim of disorder.

# U5-C04 - Ludwig Boltzmann and James Clerk Maxwell

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Connect microscopic motion to macroscopic gas properties; read a speed distribution; use a small counting model to explain multiplicity; distinguish statistical entropy from a vague claim of disorder.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## A gas looks smooth because it contains many particles
A pressure gauge gives a fairly steady reading even though gas molecules strike a wall at many separate times. A thermometer gives one temperature even though particles do not all have the same speed. Kinetic theory links these macroscopic measurements to microscopic motion. A macroscopic property describes the sample at the scale of a laboratory measurement; a microscopic description refers to individual particles and their states.

The challenge is enormous: even a small gas sample contains too many particles to follow individually. Statistical reasoning asks about distributions and likely collective behavior instead. It does not mean abandoning physical laws or guessing without evidence. It means using a description appropriate to a large population, much as a class’s score distribution contains more information than its average alone.

## Maxwell: replace a single speed with a distribution
James Clerk Maxwell lived from 1831 to 1879. Alongside his work on electromagnetism, he developed a statistical treatment of gases. His 1860 papers on the dynamical theory of gases introduced the molecular velocity distribution associated with his name. Later work by Maxwell and Boltzmann developed the subject further. The combined name Maxwell–Boltzmann does not prove they wrote one joint paper or performed one shared experiment. [H10,H11]

In an equilibrium gas, some particles move slowly, many have intermediate speeds, and some move very fast. Collisions change individual speeds and directions; a particle is not assigned permanently to a “fast group.” At steady temperature the distribution can remain stable even while its individual members change. This is a powerful distinction between an unchanging statistical pattern and frozen microscopic motion.

Read a speed graph carefully. The horizontal axis shows speed, not temperature. The vertical axis indicates the number or fraction in a speed interval, or a density that must be interpreted with the interval width. For equal-width histogram bins, taller bars mean more particles in that interval. The most populated bin is not automatically the average speed, and the largest individual speed is not the position of the peak.

For the same ideal-gas species, raising temperature shifts the distribution toward higher speeds and broadens it. Some slow particles remain; not every hot-gas particle is faster than every cooler-gas particle. The curves overlap. Comparing different gases adds the effect of molecular mass: equal temperature means equal average translational kinetic energy in the ideal-gas model, not equal speed distributions for all species. No speed formula or calculus is needed for these comparisons.

## Boltzmann: probability and the second law
Ludwig Boltzmann lived from 1844 to 1906 and worked extensively on kinetic theory and the statistical foundations of thermodynamics. His 1877 paper connected entropy to the number of microscopic possibilities compatible with a macroscopic description. [H12,H13] This added a microscopic explanation to the entropy framework associated with Clausius; it did not erase the macroscopic theory or claim that energy conservation had become optional.

A macrostate specifies coarse properties, such as how many particles occupy each half of a box. A microstate gives the detailed assignment of individual labeled particles in our simplified model. Real microscopic states also involve positions and momenta, but a left/right model is enough to illustrate multiplicity, the number of compatible detailed arrangements. The labels are bookkeeping devices in this teaching model, not a derivation of quantum statistics.

Take four independent labeled tokens A, B, C and D. Each is equally likely to be in either half of a box. There are 2×2×2×2=16 possible assignments. Only one puts all four on the left. Six put two on each side: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD or CD on the left, with the others on the right. The balanced macrostate is more likely than the specified all-left macrostate because more detailed assignments produce it, not because each particle “wants balance.”

## What a tiny model can and cannot prove
The model demonstrates why counting possibilities matters. It does not say that four tokens will always split evenly. Indeed, ten of the sixteen assignments are not exactly two-and-two. When enormous numbers of particles are considered, relative deviations from the most probable bulk behavior become much smaller. That is why ordinary gas expansion and mixing have a reliable natural direction on everyday scales even though microscopic descriptions are statistical.

Entropy is related to the multiplicity of accessible microscopic states subject to physical constraints. “Disorder” can be an informal memory aid, but visual messiness is not a measurement of entropy. A shuffled-looking picture might conceal strong constraints, while a smooth-looking gas can have an enormous number of microscopic arrangements. Energy, volume, particle number and the specified model matter. This unit uses counting and qualitative comparisons rather than a logarithmic entropy formula.

Boltzmann’s constant k_B links a per-particle energy scale to thermodynamic temperature. Its SI value is exactly 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K; k_B T therefore has energy units. It is not itself a temperature, and k_B T is not a universal formula for the entire internal energy of any object. [H04] The modern notation and metrological definition are later refinements, so the constant’s name should not be read as a claim that Boltzmann personally established every modern detail.

## Maxwell’s demon: inspect a hidden boundary
Maxwell described a selective molecular gatekeeper in an 1867 letter; the thought experiment appeared publicly in his 1871 book Theory of Heat. [H14] Imagine a tiny agent that allows faster particles toward one side and slower particles toward the other. Starting from a uniform gas, such sorting seems to create a hot side and a cold side without the usual work requirement. That apparent loophole probes what the second law assumes about microscopic control.

The demon is a thought experiment, not a real creature discovered in a gas. A complete modern account must include the physical controller, its information handling and its restoration for repeated operation. Looking only at the sorted gas hides part of the entropy accounting. It is too simple to claim that merely looking always supplies a fixed amount of heat; measurement, storage, feedback and resetting must be treated as a complete physical process. This unit asks only for the boundary insight, not advanced information-thermodynamics equations.

## Connections to previous units and applications
In Unit 1, temperature was a collective property rather than the speed of one molecule. In Unit 2, gas pressure arose from particle interactions with boundaries. Unit 3’s conduction can be interpreted through microscopic energy exchange. Unit 4’s entropy constraints now gain a statistical perspective. These are teaching connections among concepts, not a claim that the four units were discovered in that order.

Diffusion of an odor through air and the persistence of a stable thermometer reading despite collisions illustrate why distributions are useful. A simulation can follow many particles or tokens, but its rules must be stated. An artificial rule that pushes every token toward balance would bake the conclusion into the model rather than demonstrate how counting produces a probability difference.

## Visual model
![Two illustrative equal-width speed histograms each contain 100 particles. The warmer sample has more in the faster bins, but the ranges overlap. A separate four-token diagram counts all left/right macrostates.](figures/U5-C04.svg)

Two illustrative equal-width speed histograms each contain 100 particles. The warmer sample has more in the faster bins, but the ranges overlap. A separate four-token diagram counts all left/right macrostates.

## Important terminology
Kinetic theory: particle-motion account of bulk behavior. Distribution: how a population is spread over values. Macrostate: coarse description. Microstate: detailed state consistent with a model. Multiplicity: number of compatible microstates. Boltzmann constant: energy-per-temperature conversion constant, J/K. Thought experiment: reasoning through a hypothetical arrangement.

## Worked example: Count an illustrative macrostate

**Given:** Four independent labeled tokens each have two equally likely sides. Six assignments have two on each side.

**Find:** Probability of a two-and-two split.

**Formula:** Probability=favorable assignments/total assignments.

**Substitution:** p=6/2⁴.

**Calculation:** 2⁴=16; 6/16=0.375.

**Final answer:** p=37.5%.

**Physical interpretation:** The balanced macrostate is the single most numerous category, but is not guaranteed in a four-token trial.

## Worked example: Read a speed-bin table

**Given:** A toy sample of 100 particles has 8,32,40,16,4 particles in five ascending equal-width speed bins.

**Find:** Fraction in the two fastest bins.

**Formula:** Fraction=(count in selected bins)/(total count).

**Substitution:** (16+4)/100.

**Calculation:** 20/100=0.20.

**Final answer:** 20% are in the two fastest bins.

**Physical interpretation:** The distribution gives information hidden by a single temperature reading. These are illustrative counts, not Maxwell’s measured data.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
Equal temperature does not mean equal speed for every particle. Maxwell and Boltzmann did not jointly discover every named result. Boltzmann did not first introduce the term entropy. More probable does not mean certain for a tiny sample. Maxwell’s demon does not demonstrate a free, endlessly repeatable violation of the second law.

## Application and safe investigation
Use four labeled paper tokens and fair coin flips to assign left/right positions, repeating trials without selectively discarding outcomes. Compare observed frequencies with the 16 equally likely assignments; differences in a short trial are expected. Keep tokens on a desk rather than treating loose beads or gases as a required physical experiment. A data-only alternative uses the supplied assignment table.

## Chapter summary
Maxwell’s gas theory used distributions rather than one molecular speed. Boltzmann connected thermodynamic behavior and entropy to microscopic possibilities. Simple counting builds intuition, while careful system boundaries prevent the demon thought experiment from becoming a false perpetual-motion claim.

## Chapter review
1. How can a stable distribution coexist with changing molecular speeds?
2. Why does multiplicity refer to a macrostate rather than the visual neatness of a picture?
3. What must a complete account of Maxwell’s demon include?

## Practice
[WS32](../worksheets/WS32.md) includes eight questions from recognition to evidence-based reasoning.

## Mastery checklist
- [ ] I can interpret overlapping speed distributions.
- [ ] I can count the 16 assignments and explain the six balanced cases.
- [ ] I can distinguish statistical explanation from a guaranteed tiny-sample outcome.

## Historical evidence
H10: Maxwell’s original 1860 paper metadata; H11: MacTutor Maxwell biography; H12: translation of Boltzmann’s 1877 paper; H13: MacTutor Boltzmann biography; H14: APS history of Maxwell’s demon; H04: BIPM constant definition.

Full bibliographic details, links and attribution limits: [Unit 5 source guide](../references/U5-sources.md).

chapters.content_markdown:
# U5-C05 - Historical Development and Scientific Connections

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Place major developments in order; explain how experiments and theories corrected or extended earlier ideas; evaluate claims about priority and collaboration; connect all eight scientists to modern thermodynamics.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## A history of problems, not a parade of names
Learning history is more useful when each name answers a scientific question. What does a thermometer tell us? Why can ice melt without warming? Can mechanical motion produce a predictable thermal change? What limits an engine? Why do ordinary processes have a preferred direction? What does a gas’s temperature mean for its molecules? Why does hot matter emit the spectrum it does? The scientists in this unit addressed different parts of this connected set of problems.

The order of discovery is not identical to the order of a modern textbook. Carnot’s engine analysis appeared before Joule’s mature experimental program and before the modern first law was established. Black’s useful thermal distinctions preceded an energy-based explanation. Maxwell and Boltzmann developed statistical accounts after important macroscopic principles were already in place. Teaching the completed theory first helps us interpret the history, but it must not make the past look inevitable.

## Begin with measurements: Black to calorimetry
Black’s eighteenth-century work helped separate temperature from the energy associated with a thermal change. Melting and warming could not be understood by reading a thermometer alone. Specific heat and latent heat provided ways to compare the effects of energy transfers on different materials and phases. The problem was quantitative even before the modern language of joules and internal energy became standard.

This is a conceptual foundation for later calorimetry. If a scientist wants to compare mechanical input with a thermal effect, that thermal effect must be measured reliably. However, a conceptual foundation is not proof of a direct collaboration. Black died in 1799, before Joule was born in 1818. It would be historically false to stage a shared laboratory conversation between them. A classroom dialogue can be used only if clearly labeled fictional; this unit instead uses explanatory connections.

## Engines and the revision of an inherited model
Carnot’s 1824 engine theory pursued a limit, not merely a better component. A powerful feature of such reasoning is that an ideal comparison can constrain many real machines. Yet his published analysis retained caloric assumptions. Joule’s work-to-warming evidence contributed to a new account in which energy is conserved while heat and work are interchangeable transfer modes.

The later synthesis did not require throwing away every part of Carnot’s reasoning. Clausius and Thomson helped preserve the reversible-engine insight while correcting its energy interpretation. Clapeyron’s 1834 reformulation was one historical route by which Carnot’s work became better known. These relationships are supported in the historical sources. They show how an idea can be reformulated, circulated and corrected, rather than simply accepted or rejected as a whole.

## Absolute temperature connects measurement to theory
Thomson’s 1848 proposal belongs in this sequence, but it should not be treated as the final modern Kelvin definition. Temperature-scale development interacted with engine reasoning and the emerging dynamical theory of heat. Today the absolute scale allows consistent ideal-gas and engine-efficiency ratios. A formula written with T in Kelvin is not merely using a different label for Celsius; it is relying on an absolute zero.

Joule and Thomson also carried out documented gas investigations together. This is an actual collaborative relationship, unlike the looser claim that every paired name in this workbook represents a shared laboratory. When discussing influence, ask what evidence is available: a joint investigation, a published citation, a reformulation, or simply a useful connection made by a modern teacher. These are different kinds of statements and deserve different wording.

## Conservation and entropy answer complementary questions
By the middle nineteenth century, thermal theory increasingly distinguished energy accounting from process direction. Clausius’s development of entropy, named in 1865, provided a state quantity for the second-law discussion. A complete cycle returns the working substance to its original state, while its surroundings can change. This prevents a cyclic engine from being judged solely by one favorable stroke.

The first law and second law do not compete. An engine that creates energy fails the first. An energy-balanced cyclic engine that turns all heat from a single reservoir into work with no other effect fails the second. Similarly, saying a warm cup and cooler room exchange equal amounts of energy does not establish which direction is natural. A history answer becomes stronger when it explains this conceptual need instead of merely listing “Clausius: entropy.”

## From molecules to probabilities
Maxwell’s 1860 gas-distribution work replaced a single typical molecular speed with a population description. Boltzmann’s statistical reasoning connected accessible microscopic possibilities to entropy, notably in 1877. The macroscopic laws remained useful; statistics offered a route to explaining why large collections behave so reliably. That bridge is central to modern thermal physics.

Do not confuse a later named formula with a single isolated moment of invention. The name Maxwell–Boltzmann recognizes connected contributions to a developing subject. Clausius supplied an important macroscopic entropy framework; Boltzmann supplied a statistical interpretation. The modern constant named for Boltzmann also appears in temperature measurement and radiation theory. Naming conventions compress a complicated history and should be expanded when attribution matters.

## Radiation takes the story beyond classical physics
Planck’s 1900 radiation work drew on thermodynamic and statistical ideas while introducing energy elements into the explanation of a measured spectrum. It was not a discovery that hot objects radiate; that was already known. The achievement concerned the quantitative form and physical account of the radiation distribution. The later photon interpretation and full quantum mechanics involved additional scientists and developments.

This sequence shows both continuity and correction. Energy conservation remained essential. Entropy and statistics remained useful. But a classical description of all microscopic energy exchange was not enough for the radiation problem. New evidence constrained the model, and new concepts were developed. In modern science, a theory can be extremely successful within a domain without being the final explanation at every scale.

## How to read and verify a timeline
A timeline entry needs an event as well as a date. A birth date, lecture date, publication date and award date cannot be substituted for one another. Black’s 1762 presentation and 1803 posthumous lectures are different events. Planck’s 1900 work and 1918 Nobel Prize are different events. Maxwell’s distribution papers and demon thought experiment are different contributions even though both involve molecules.

Dates should be precise only when the evidence supports that precision. The 1840s is appropriate for Joule’s broad experimental program; attaching one year to every experiment would falsely compress a series. A museum’s later apparatus can illustrate an earlier method, but its catalog date should remain visible. A historian’s retrospective summary is useful, while a primary source helps reveal the language and assumptions of the period. Neither should be copied without context.

## Use the connected history in competition reasoning
An unfamiliar question may describe evidence rather than name a scientist. Start by identifying the physical issue. A melting plateau points toward latent heat and Black. A work input producing controlled warming points toward Joule. A reversible upper limit points toward Carnot and its later thermodynamic interpretation. Entropy’s naming points toward Clausius; its statistical interpretation toward Boltzmann. A molecular speed distribution points toward Maxwell. Absolute-temperature development points toward Kelvin. Discrete energy elements in a radiation explanation point toward Planck.

Some prompts correctly require more than one name. Explain the separate roles rather than forcing a single answer. A calorimetric test of an engine links thermal measurement, energy conservation and efficiency limits. A radiation problem can connect Planck’s energy elements with statistical reasoning. These are connections among tools, not evidence that all eight scientists worked as one team.

## The continuing importance of these questions
Thermodynamics informs heat pumps, engines, materials, atmospheric processes, electronics and measurement standards. The history matters because it teaches how to test explanations: define the system, measure the relevant quantities, state assumptions, compare competing predictions and track what a result actually establishes. In the later device unit, a temperature gain will likewise be evidence about a particular experiment, not proof that every proposed model of the device is correct.

## Visual model
![A dated timeline runs from Black’s eighteenth-century work through Planck’s 1900 breakthrough. The date labels identify distinct developments; spacing is not proportional to elapsed time.](figures/U5-C05.svg)

A dated timeline runs from Black’s eighteenth-century work through Planck’s 1900 breakthrough. The date labels identify distinct developments; spacing is not proportional to elapsed time.

## Important terminology
Chronology: ordering by time. Primary source: evidence from the period or investigator. Historical interpretation: later analysis of that evidence. Refinement: improved version of an idea. Conceptual connection: relationship between ideas, not automatically personal contact. Attribution: assigning credit accurately and with appropriate limits.

## Worked example: Separate a discovery from its award

**Given:** Planck’s radiation breakthrough: 1900; Nobel Prize: 1918.

**Find:** Elapsed calendar years.

**Formula:** Interval=later year−earlier year.

**Substitution:** 1918−1900.

**Calculation:** 18.

**Final answer:** 18 years.

**Physical interpretation:** A later award recognizes earlier work; the dates label different events.

## Worked example: Apply two laws to one historical-style claim

**Given:** Engine: Q_H=1000 J, W=600 J, Q_C=400 J; T_H=500 K, T_C=300 K.

**Find:** Whether the ledger and ideal limit both pass.

**Formula:** Q_H=W+Q_C; η=W/Q_H; η_max=1−T_C/T_H.

**Substitution:** 600+400=1000; η=600/1000; η_max=1−300/500.

**Calculation:** Ledger balances; η=0.60; η_max=0.40.

**Final answer:** Conserves energy but exceeds the 40% bound.

**Physical interpretation:** Joule-associated conservation is necessary; Carnot/Clausius-associated limits add a separate restriction.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
A modern equation beside a scientist’s name does not prove that person wrote it in today’s form. A discovery date is not a birthday or prize date. Being influential does not mean working alone. A conceptual arrow does not prove a meeting. An earlier model can contain a useful observation and an incorrect explanation at the same time.

## Application and safe investigation
Use the separate timeline and comparison chart to build an evidence board: each claim gets a date, contribution and source ID. Ask students to correct an intentionally misleading museum caption. Keep all classroom data labeled illustrative and all invented scenarios labeled hypothetical. This practice prepares students to explain unfamiliar evidence rather than memorize a fixed list.

## Comparing all eight contributions
| Scientist | Contribution | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joseph Black | Specific heat; latent heat | Separated temperature from thermal quantity; foundation for calorimetry. |
| Sadi Carnot | Ideal reversible engine reasoning | Established roots of a general performance limit; original caloric framework later revised. |
| James Prescott Joule | Mechanical equivalent of heat | Quantitative experimental support for energy conversion and conservation. |
| Rudolf Clausius | Second-law development; entropy | Added direction and irreversibility to energy accounting. |
| William Thomson / Lord Kelvin | Absolute temperature; thermodynamic theory | Developed a general temperature framework; original proposal later refined. |
| James Clerk Maxwell | Molecular velocity distribution; demon | Connected particle populations with bulk properties; examined second-law assumptions. |
| Ludwig Boltzmann | Statistical interpretation of entropy | Explained thermal regularities through microscopic possibilities. |
| Max Planck | Radiation law; energy quanta | Opened quantum theory through the thermal-radiation problem. |

## Chapter summary
Thermodynamics developed through measurements, idealizations, disagreements and revisions. Black’s thermal distinctions, Carnot’s limits, Joule’s equivalence, Kelvin’s scale, Clausius’s entropy, Maxwell’s distributions, Boltzmann’s statistics and Planck’s quanta address connected but distinct problems. Accurate history explains both the contribution and its limits.

## Chapter review
1. Why does Carnot appearing before Joule complicate a simple textbook-order timeline?
2. What evidence distinguishes a collaboration from a teaching connection?
3. How can a model be corrected while part of its reasoning survives?

## Practice
[WS33](../worksheets/WS33.md) includes eight questions from recognition to evidence-based reasoning.

## Mastery checklist
- [ ] I can place the main developments in order and label what each date means.
- [ ] I can explain all eight contributions with their physical significance.
- [ ] I can identify and correct unsupported collaboration and sole-discoverer claims.

## Historical evidence
H01–H14 support the chronology and named contributions; the separate source guide maps specific claims to references. Modern worked examples are original illustrations, not historical records.

Full bibliographic details, links and attribution limits: [Unit 5 source guide](../references/U5-sources.md).

# Unit 5 scientist comparison chart

public-student | All competition levels

The equations are modern associations, not a claim that each individual wrote the modern formula alone. Life dates provide context; contribution dates belong in the timeline.

| Scientist and lifespan | Contribution | Modern concept and significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joseph Black (1728–1799) | Specific heat; latent heat | Separated temperature from thermal quantity; foundation for calorimetry. Q=mcΔT; Q=mL (modern notation) [H01,H02] |
| Sadi Carnot (1796–1832) | Ideal reversible engine reasoning | Established roots of a general performance limit; original caloric framework later revised. Modern η_max=1−T_C/T_H [H06] |
| James Prescott Joule (1818–1889) | Mechanical equivalent of heat | Quantitative experimental support for energy conversion and conservation. ΔU=Q−W; joule J [H05] |
| Rudolf Clausius (1822–1888) | Second-law development; entropy | Added direction and irreversibility to energy accounting. Total isolated entropy cannot decrease [H07] |
| William Thomson / Lord Kelvin (1824–1907) | Absolute temperature; thermodynamic theory | Developed a general temperature framework; original proposal later refined. T=t+273.15; Kelvin ratios [H03,H04] |
| James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) | Molecular velocity distribution; demon | Connected particle populations with bulk properties; examined second-law assumptions. Statistical gas description [H10,H11,H14] |
| Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906) | Statistical interpretation of entropy | Explained thermal regularities through microscopic possibilities. Multiplicity; k_B links energy and K [H12,H13,H04] |
| Max Planck (1858–1947) | Radiation law; energy quanta | Opened quantum theory through the thermal-radiation problem. ε=hf conceptually [H08,H09] |

## Three attribution checks
Clausius named entropy; Boltzmann developed its statistical interpretation. Kelvin’s scale concerns absolute temperature; Black’s latent heat concerns energy during phase change. Joule’s conservation evidence and Carnot’s ideal limits answer different questions.

# Unit 5 discoveries and equations reference

public-student | All competition levels | Modern notation with historical limits

## Black: material response and phase change
Q=mcΔT applies to sensible heating with an appropriate approximately constant c and no phase change. Q is J; m is kg; c is J/(kg·K); ΔT is K or a Celsius difference. Q=mL applies to the stated phase change, with L in J/kg. For 0.10 kg water, c=4200 J/(kg·K) and ΔT=2 K, Q=840 J. For 0.010 kg melting ice with L=334000 J/kg, Q=3340 J. These modern relationships express distinctions associated with Black; they are not a transcription of his notation. Heat capacity C=mc (J/K) differs from conductivity (W/(m·K)).

## Kelvin: an absolute temperature framework
T=t+273.15 converts Celsius t to Kelvin T. At 0 °C, T=273.15 K. A 5 °C temperature change is 5 K, but a ratio of Celsius readings is not an absolute-temperature ratio. Kelvin’s 1848 proposal and the present SI definition are different historical stages.

## Joule: conservation in common energy units
ΔU=Q−W uses heat into a closed system as positive Q and work by it as positive W; neglect bulk kinetic and potential energy changes. A 100 J work input with Q=0 means W=−100 J and ΔU=+100 J. One J equals one N·m. The first law had multiple contributors; Joule supplied major quantitative experimental evidence.

## Carnot: actual performance versus a modern reversible limit
W_net=Q_H−Q_C and η=W_net/Q_H use positive heat magnitudes. The modern ideal bound is η_max=1−T_C/T_H, with Kelvin reservoir temperatures. Between 600 K and 300 K the ceiling is 50%. Carnot’s original published caloric framework did not use the complete modern energy interpretation. The bound is a limit, not a guarantee of actual performance.

## Clausius: entropy and direction
For an isolated total, ΔS_total≥0. S has units J/K, not J. A reversible ideal process gives zero total change; an irreversible one gives a positive change. Local decreases are possible. Adding supplied changes −1 and +2 J/K gives a total +1 J/K. No advanced entropy formula is required here.

## Maxwell: distributions, not one universal molecular speed
The number in a bin divided by the total gives that bin’s fraction. In a 100-particle teaching table, 25 particles in a bin means 25%. Equal-width bins allow direct height comparisons. A stable distribution does not imply motionless particles, and hotter distributions can overlap cooler ones.

## Boltzmann: multiplicity and a temperature-energy link
Count compatible arrangements under stated assumptions. Four independent two-choice labeled tokens give 2⁴=16 assignments. Six are balanced two-and-two, so their combined probability is 6/16=37.5%. This is a finite teaching analogy, not a derivation of gas entropy. k_B has units J/K; k_B T has energy units. No logarithmic entropy calculation is assessed.

## Planck: discrete energy elements
ε=hf expresses the conceptual relation between an energy element ε (J), frequency f (Hz) and Planck’s constant h (J·s). Doubling f doubles ε at fixed h. This does not determine total lamp power. The oscillator-energy contribution is distinguished from later photon theory. Detailed radiation calculations remain State/National Unit 6; no numerical quantum calculation is assigned in this unit.
references.U5-historical-connections:
# Unit 5 historical connections study guide

public-student | All competition levels

## Start with the physical problem
A good response has three parts: identify the problem, describe the contribution, and explain why it changed understanding. A fourth part can state its historical limit. For example: a thermometer failed to show the energy absorbed during melting; Black developed latent-heat reasoning; this separated phase energy from temperature change; his historical language was not modern internal-energy terminology.

## Measurement supports conservation
Black-associated calorimetry provides methods for measuring thermal effects. Joule’s mechanical experiments compare such effects with work input. This is a conceptual dependency, not a collaboration: Black died before Joule was born. Connect their ideas without inventing a meeting or letter.

## A successful insight can survive a failed framework
Carnot analyzed reversible engine limits within caloric theory. The later energy theory changed the interpretation of absorbed and rejected heat. Clausius and Thomson incorporated the engine insights into mature thermodynamics; Clapeyron’s reformulation helped communicate them. The correction preserved useful reasoning while replacing an assumption.

## Two laws answer two questions
Joule-associated evidence helps explain why energy amounts balance. Clausius’s second-law and entropy work explains why an energy-balanced process can still be forbidden. Carnot’s modern upper bound applies these limits to engines. Kelvin temperatures are necessary in the bound because ratios need an absolute zero.

## From bulk measurements to particle populations
Maxwell used distributions to describe molecular motion. Boltzmann connected entropy to microscopic possibilities. Neither approach requires all particles to have the same speed. The thermodynamic state remains a useful bulk description even when the microscopic details are continually changing.

## Radiation links classical thermodynamics to quantum ideas
Planck used thermal and statistical ideas in the radiation-spectrum problem. Introducing energy elements was a new step; it did not erase conservation or make every earlier theory useless. Einstein’s later light-quantum work and later quantum mechanics developed the account further. Do not describe the entire field as one completed discovery in 1900.

## Distinguish kinds of connection
Documented collaboration: Joule and Thomson’s gas work [H03]. Documented reformulation and influence: Clapeyron’s treatment of Carnot and later Clausius/Thomson synthesis [H06,H07]. Conceptual comparison: Black’s melting plateau and Planck’s spectral problem both expose limits of simple models, but this does not establish personal contact. A named distribution is not by itself proof of a jointly authored experiment.

## Study method
For each of the eight scientists, write one problem-contribution-significance sentence. Then explain one connection and label it historical or conceptual. Finally, check a source ID for a major date. Use WS33 to test whether you can reason from unfamiliar evidence rather than merely recite names.

# Unit 5 common confusions reference

public-student | All competition levels

| Confusion | Correction and reason |
| --- | --- |
| Kelvin and Black both discovered heat. | Kelvin developed absolute-temperature ideas; Black clarified specific and latent heat. Neither broad phrase captures their separate contributions. |
| Same temperature means the same thermal energy. | Mass, material and phase matter. A thermometer alone does not provide an energy total. |
| A melting plateau means no heat enters. | Energy can drive a phase change with little temperature change. |
| Joule’s paddles supply heat through the shaft. | For the water system the shaft supplies work. Warming describes the result, not the transfer mode. |
| Carnot wrote today’s complete energy theory in 1824. | His published framework used caloric assumptions; later thermodynamics revised the energy interpretation. |
| Any engine below 100% is feasible. | It must also respect the reservoir-dependent Carnot bound and other physical constraints. |
| Clausius and Boltzmann both first named entropy. | Clausius named entropy in 1865; Boltzmann developed its statistical interpretation, notably in 1877. |
| Entropy is energy that was destroyed. | Entropy is a state property in J/K. Energy is conserved even when useful work potential decreases. |
| Every molecule at one temperature has the same speed. | Temperature describes collective behavior; equilibrium gases have distributions. |
| Maxwell–Boltzmann proves a shared paper. | The name recognizes connected contributions and is not evidence of coauthorship. |
| The demon is a proven perpetual-motion machine. | It is a thought experiment. Include the physical controller and repeated restoration in the full accounting. |
| Planck invented the word entropy. | His key contribution here concerns radiation and energy quanta; Clausius introduced entropy. |
| 1900 and 1918 are interchangeable Planck dates. | 1900 labels the breakthrough; 1918 labels the Nobel Prize. |
| Blackbody means no emission. | It is an ideal absorber and thermal emitter; sufficiently hot examples glow. |
| A diagram proves historical collaboration. | A conceptual map can show related ideas without documenting personal interaction. |

glossary.Absolute scale: Temperature scale referenced to absolute zero; use Kelvin for thermodynamic ratios.
glossary.Caloric theory: Historical model treating heat as a conserved substance.
glossary.Energy quantum: Discrete energy element in a specified physical model.
glossary.Entropy: State property in J/K used in second-law reasoning.
glossary.Heat capacity: Sample coefficient in J/K; generally depends on mass.
glossary.Specific heat capacity: Material coefficient in J/(kg·K) under specified conditions.
glossary.Latent heat: Energy transfer associated with a phase change rather than a temperature rise.
glossary.Macrostate: Coarse bulk description of a system.
glossary.Microstate: Detailed microscopic state within a specified model.
glossary.Primary source: Evidence originating with the investigator or period.
glossary.Reversible process: Ideal limit that can be undone without net effects on system and surroundings.
glossary.Spectrum: Distribution of radiation across frequencies or wavelengths.
glossary.Statistical model: Description using populations and probabilities rather than every trajectory.
glossary.Thermal reservoir: Ideal body maintaining nearly constant temperature during heat exchange.
glossary.Thought experiment: Hypothetical physical scenario used to examine reasoning.
glossary.Frequency: Oscillations per second, measured in Hz.
glossary.Refinement: A later improvement or correction to an earlier account.
