# Unit 5 review

public-student | All competition levels

## Retrieval routine
Explain each contribution as problem → evidence or reasoning → contribution → significance. Use the timeline for dates, the comparison chart for distinctions, and the equation reference for modern connections. A correct name alone is not a complete scientific explanation.

## Review questions
1. Explain how Black’s work undermines the claim that a thermometer measures all transferred energy.
2. Explain why Kelvin temperatures are required in an engine-limit ratio.
3. Follow the energy from falling weights to a warmer stirred sample.
4. Identify what modern theory retained and corrected in Carnot’s work.
5. Distinguish Clausius’s entropy contribution from Boltzmann’s.
6. Explain why Maxwell’s distribution does not assign a fixed speed to every molecule.
7. State what was new about Planck’s radiation contribution without attributing all later quantum theory to him.
8. Give one documented historical relationship and one clearly labeled conceptual connection.

## Readiness
Correct confusion about energy versus entropy, heat versus work, dates versus recognition dates, and historical versus conceptual relationships before proceeding. The next unit treats detailed radiation and the third law as State/National content. History remains all-level.
source_guide_markdown:
# Unit 5 historical evidence and source guide

public-student | Checked 2026-10-18 UTC | Original instructional writing

## How evidence is used
Historical sources establish dates, attributions and documented relationships. The physical examples, numerical data, diagrams and classroom scenarios are original educational models, not claimed historical measurements. No historical quotations are invented or reproduced. This unit is a teaching synthesis, not an exhaustive scholarly history. Primary texts retain obsolete terminology; modern explanations explicitly translate it. University histories, museum collections, Nobel archives and the SI authority provide context or verification.

## H01
University of Edinburgh, School of Chemistry. Joseph Black (1728–1799).

https://chem.ed.ac.uk/about-us/history/professors/joseph-black

Life dates; Glasgow investigations; 1762 presentation. Institutional history.

## H02
Joseph Black. Lectures on the Elements of Chemistry, edited posthumously by John Robison (1803). Excerpts hosted by Le Moyne College, from Magie’s Source Book.

https://webserver.lemoyne.edu/giunta/blackheat.html

Primary-source excerpts: distinction between temperature and thermal quantity, material heat capacities and melting observations. Old terminology is translated, not adopted as modern physics.

## H03
MacTutor, University of St Andrews. William Thomson (1824–1907).

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Thomson/

Biographical context; 1848 temperature-scale proposal; development of thermodynamics and Joule collaboration.

## H04
BIPM. SI base unit: kelvin.

https://www.bipm.org/en/si-base-units/kelvin

Authoritative modern definition and exact Boltzmann constant, 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K. Not a description of Kelvin’s 1848 definition.

## H05
Science and Industry Museum. James Joule’s radical ideas about energy; Science Museum Group paddlewheel catalog.

https://blog.scienceandindustrymuseum.org.uk/james-joules-energy/

Joule’s work-to-warming experimental program. Companion object record: https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co8404691/paddlewheel-used-by-james-joule ; this particular apparatus is dated c.1860, not the first experiment.

## H06
MacTutor, University of St Andrews. Sadi Carnot (1796–1832).

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Carnot_Sadi/

1824 book, caloric setting, 1834 Clapeyron reformulation and later Clausius/Thomson interpretation.

## H07
MacTutor, University of St Andrews. Rudolf Clausius (1822–1888).

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Clausius/

1850 mechanical theory of heat paper; entropy development and naming in 1865.

## H08
NobelPrize.org. Max Planck: Facts.

https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1918/planck/facts/

Life dates, 1900 work and 1918 award. These dates refer to different events.

## H09
NobelPrize.org. The dual nature of light as reflected in the Nobel archives.

https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/the-dual-nature-of-light-as-reflected-in-the-nobel-archives/

Distinguishes Planck’s energy-quanta contribution from the later light-quantum interpretation and particle-nature attribution.

## H10
James Clerk Maxwell. Illustrations of the dynamical theory of gases, Part I (1860), Philosophical Magazine 19. DOI: 10.1080/14786446008642818.

https://doi.org/10.1080/14786446008642818

Primary-paper bibliographic record confirms author, title and original 1860 publication; later online publication metadata is not the original date.

## H11
MacTutor, University of St Andrews. James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879).

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Maxwell/

Life context and development of kinetic theory alongside electromagnetism. Used with the original-paper date.

## H12
Ludwig Boltzmann (1877), translated by Kim Sharp and Franz Matschinsky (2015). On the Relationship between the Second Fundamental Theorem of the Mechanical Theory of Heat and Probability Calculations Regarding the Conditions for Thermal Equilibrium. Entropy 17, 1971–2009.

https://doi.org/10.3390/e17041971

Translation of a primary work on probability and entropy. Distinguish the 1877 original from the 2015 translation.

## H13
MacTutor, University of St Andrews. Ludwig Boltzmann (1844–1906).

https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Boltzmann/

Life dates and kinetic/statistical research context.

## H14
American Physical Society. June 1871: Maxwell and His Demon.

https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2002/06/maxwell

1867 private thought-experiment communication and 1871 public treatment; historical context for a conceptual boundary discussion.

## Attribution limits
The eight required scientists were not the only contributors to thermodynamics. A formula associated with a scientist may have modern notation or later refinements. Carnot’s 1824 caloric setting is distinguished from modern conservation and the Kelvin-based bound. Thomson’s first absolute-scale proposal is distinguished from the current SI definition. Clausius’s naming of entropy is distinguished from Boltzmann’s statistical interpretation. Planck’s energy elements are distinguished from Einstein’s later light-quantum proposal. Maxwell–Boltzmann is not treated as proof of a coauthored paper.

## Rules scope
The supplied 2027 Division B manual, printed B57, 5.c.v lists all eight historical contributors. This unit provides all-level historical context. Detailed blackbody, radiant-exitance, Stefan–Boltzmann and third-law content is separately State/National-only under 5.c.vi and remains Unit 6. Exercises follow 5.d: arithmetic, ratios, exponents, one-variable algebra and elementary counting. No logarithmic entropy calculation, calculus, trigonometry or advanced probability is required. The protected manual is not redistributed. No claim is made that later rule clarifications have been checked.
